original_question: Does there exist a non-Riemannian Finsler metric satisfying the Landsberg condition on a surface of genus ≥ 2?
target_in_paper: Question 10.1.4 in §10.1, "Metrics with integrable geodesic flow on surfaces of genus ≥ 2."
correct_elements: The draft already matches the paper's actual target almost verbatim: it asks for the existence of a non-Riemannian Finsler metric satisfying the Landsberg condition on a surface of genus at least 2. These are exactly the essential ingredients of Question 10.1.4.
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, the surface should be specified as closed; this is explicit in the immediately preceding Questions 10.1.1 and 10.1.3 in the same subsection and is part of the subsection's ambient setup.
The paper's standing convention is that the manifold is connected and C∞, so the smooth category is implicit and should be stated explicitly in a self-contained version.
The existential quantifier is over a pair (M, F): a surface M of genus ≥ 2 together with a Finsler metric F on M, rather than over an unspecified fixed surface.
For clarity, 'non-Riemannian' should be read as 'not induced by any Riemannian metric.'

The paper does not restate the definition of the Landsberg condition locally in this subsection; it treats it as standard Finsler terminology and refers externally for the definition, so that definition remains implicit in the paper's own wording.
refined_question: Does there exist a connected closed C∞ surface M of genus g ≥ 2 carrying a non-Riemannian C∞ Finsler metric F that satisfies the Landsberg condition?
justification: Your draft is already essentially the paper's official formulation: Question 10.1.4 asks exactly this existence question. The only changes needed to make it fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper's scope are to restore the ambient conventions fixed earlier in the paper (connected C∞ manifolds) and the closed-surface setting supplied by the surrounding subsection and neighboring questions. I did not broaden the problem beyond §10.1. The paragraph immediately following Question 10.1.4 explains why it appears in the integrability section: the Landsberg condition implies the existence of an integral for the geodesic flow, and the authors also note a negative answer under the extra hypothesis of nonexistence of conjugate points.
